subject: chemistry
title: Relative atomic mass and the mole

scenes.heading: Relative atomic mass and the mole
scenes.sub: How do you count atoms you can't even see?
scenes.say: Atoms are far too small to count one by one. So chemists compare their masses, and count them in huge groups called moles.

scenes.heading: A relative scale
points: Every atom is compared with it
scenes.say: One carbon atom weighs about two times ten to the minus twenty-three grams. That's awkward! So chemists compare every atom with carbon-12, which is set at exactly twelve. It's like measuring your friends against one mate. Because it's a comparison, there are no units.
scenes.caption: One carbon atom weighs about 2 × 10⁻²³ g. That's awkward! So chemists compare every atom with carbon-12, which is set at exactly 12. It's like measuring your friends against one mate. Because it's a comparison, there are no units.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.science: Ar: a weighted average of isotope masses
scenes.breaks: A teacher chooses the weightings; isotope abundances are set by nature and measured.
scenes.say: Relative atomic mass, A R, is like a weighted average mark. Chlorine is seventy-five percent chlorine-35 and twenty-five percent chlorine-37. So its A R is thirty-five point five, closer to thirty-five. But no single chlorine atom has a mass of thirty-five point five.
scenes.caption: Relative atomic mass, Ar, is like a weighted average mark. Chlorine is 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37. So its Ar is 35.5, closer to 35. But no single chlorine atom has a mass of 35.5.

scenes.heading: Calculating Ar
scenes.question: Natural boron is 19.9% boron-10 and 80.1% boron-11. Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron.
scenes.say: Multiply each isotope's mass by its percentage, add them, and divide by a hundred. Ten times nineteen point nine, plus eleven times eighty point one, is one thousand and eighty point one. Divide by a hundred: ten point eight. It's closer to eleven, because boron-11 is far more common.
scenes.caption: Multiply each isotope's mass by its percentage, add them, and divide by 100. 10 × 19.9 + 11 × 80.1 = 1080.1. Divide by 100: 10.8. It's closer to 11, because boron-11 is far more common.

scenes.heading: The mole
points: 1 mol of water ≈ one tablespoon (18 g)
scenes.say: A mole is six point zero two times ten to the twenty-three particles. That's Avogadro's constant: a chemist's dozen. It's a huge number, yet a mole of water is only about a tablespoon, eighteen grams, because each molecule is so tiny.
scenes.caption: A mole is 6.02 × 10²³ particles. That's Avogadro's constant: a chemist's dozen. It's a huge number, yet a mole of water is only about a tablespoon, 18 g, because each molecule is so tiny.

scenes.heading: Finding molar mass
scenes.say: Here's the magic bridge: one mole weighs, in grams, the same number as its relative mass. That's the molar mass, in grams per mole. Just add up the relative atomic masses. Like a bank weighing coins, you can count atoms on a balance.

scenes.heading: Brackets multiply
scenes.question: Calculate the molar mass of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂.
scenes.say: For calcium hydroxide, the two outside the bracket multiplies everything inside. So it's one calcium, two oxygens and two hydrogens. Forty point one, plus thirty-two, plus two, gives seventy-four point one grams per mole.
scenes.caption: For Ca(OH)₂, the 2 outside the bracket multiplies everything inside: 1 Ca, 2 O and 2 H. 40.1 + 32.0 + 2.0 gives 74.1 g mol⁻¹.

points: Molar mass M in g mol⁻¹
Ar and Mr have no units
scenes.say: Quick recap. Masses are compared with carbon-12. A R is a weighted average. A mole is six point zero two times ten to the twenty-three particles, and molar mass is in grams per mole. Now try the practice questions!
